rationale: B wins because it is more disciplined about proof and danger signs. Its strongest move is the pricing angle, "Rivian is charging other automakers' drivers a premium to use its chargers," which gives a real consumer hook and immediately demands the missing price gap. A has good bones, but "Rivian fields a rival to Tesla's Supercharger network" turns a NACS/access update into a competitive claim the facts do not yet earn.
gaps_in_A: "following the industry's shift away from automaker-exclusive plugs" imports a whole industry trend from outside the update. Source it or soften it.
"Rivian fields a rival to Tesla's Supercharger network" is the riskiest overreach. NACS plus open access does not prove Rivian is fielding a Tesla rival.
"charging networks that were once brand perks are becoming shared utilities" is a trend-piece sentence built on one supplied company move. Nice line, thin footing.
The proof asks are solid, but A misses some sharper operational checks: geographic spread, whether all 3,500+ chargers are open, and how many non-Rivian sessions actually happen.
gaps_in_B: "the connector fight is over" is too cute and too broad. Dual plugs on new Rivian stalls do not end a standards fight.
"joining the small set of automaker-owned networks that sell to non-owners" may be true, but it is outside the supplied facts and needs sourcing before it becomes a premise.
"operators eating the hardware cost" asserts economics the update does not provide. Keep that as required proof, not as a conclusion.
"capital-heavy network built to sell trucks" is plausible context, but still unsupplied. B occasionally lets smart market inference walk around dressed as fact.
